questions.q: Why does the app VM get deployed into app-subnet rather than into a newly-created network?
options: Because the order of network versus compute deployment doesn't actually matter
Because Lesson 29 already deployed and verified that network, and compute lands into infrastructure that's proven to work
Because Azure requires all VMs to use the same subnet name across every project
Because app-subnet is the only subnet that supports virtual machines
questions.explain: Compute and storage deploy into the network layer only after it's been deployed and verified, following the network-first order from Chapter 2.

questions.q: How does the app VM authenticate to the storage account and the database without a stored password or key?
options: The VM uses the same password as the Microsoft 365 admin account
A system-assigned managed identity is granted the Storage Blob Data Contributor role and a matching Azure AD database user
Managed identity only works for storage accounts, so the database still needs a SQL password
The app stores the storage account key in an environment variable instead of a config file
questions.explain: A managed identity lets the VM authenticate as itself to both the storage account and the database -- there's no credential to store, leak, or rotate.

questions.q: What makes the smoke test in this lesson more than just confirming the VM is running?
options: It relies on the app's own internal health-check endpoint instead of real data
It only checks that the VM's power state shows as 'Running' in the Azure portal
It places a real test order, uploads a real test invoice, and confirms both actually land in the database and storage
It skips checking the NSGs since those were already verified in Lesson 29
questions.explain: A smoke test is an actual round trip through the data path, not a status light -- confirming data really moves end to end.

questions.q: Why does this lesson configure only four alerts instead of alerting on every available metric?
options: Because monitoring isn't actually necessary once a smoke test has passed once
To avoid alert fatigue -- a small set of high-confidence alerts is more useful than a large set that trains the on-call person to ignore them
Because Azure Monitor only supports a maximum of four alerts per subscription
Because more alerts always cost significantly more money regardless of configuration
questions.explain: Chapter 4's alert-fatigue principle drives this: fewer, well-chosen alerts that someone will actually act on beat a flood of low-value ones.

questions.q: What do all four of this lesson's configured alerts have in common?
options: They all monitor the exact same metric from different resources
They route to a public mailing list rather than a specific action group
Each one has a specific, actionable response and routes to the one person actually on call
None of them are expected to ever actually fire in production
questions.explain: Every alert maps to something actionable -- sustained CPU, low disk space, database utilization, or storage availability -- routed to one action group reaching the on-call person.
